source: Campitelli, Connors, Bilalic & Hambrick (2015) Psychological perspectives on expertise (Frontiers Research Topic editorial)
finding: Editorial for a 35-article collection. It sorts expertise research into five programmes: cognitive processes, development, expertise and general cognition, transfer of skills between domains, and methods and frameworks.
numbers: 35 articles; domains include chess, music, perception, teaching, ICU diagnosis, video games, sports, dance, maths, climbing, fingerprints.
limits: An editorial summary, not new data. Each claim is that of the cited article.
agent_relevance: Shows the field's structure. The transfer and cognitive-process strands bear on a scaffold that must work across domains.

source: Campitelli et al. (2015) editorial: eye-movement strand
finding: Four articles used eye tracking. Expert chess players quickly tell board regions relevant to the best move from irrelevant ones. Expert ICU doctors look at more relevant parts of a case than competent non-experts. Experts in arithmetic spontaneously use shortcuts. Einstellung was studied with eye movements and tied to expert flexibility.
numbers: Sheridan & Reingold; McCormack et al.; Godau et al.; Ellis & Reingold (anagram Einstellung). No effect sizes given in the editorial.
limits: Summary level only.
agent_relevance: Experts differ in where they look first, not in how long they think. Suggests a cheap relevance filter before deep work.

source: Campitelli et al. (2015) editorial: development strand (learning curves, deliberate practice)
finding: Reports an exponential, not power-law, learning curve in chess (Gaschler et al.), Gobet and Ereku's argument that Carlsen is not explained by deliberate practice alone, and Platz et al.'s music meta-analysis, which Hambrick et al. read as showing practice matters but is not the only factor.
numbers: Gaschler et al.: 1383 chess players tracked over 10 years. Platz et al.: r_c = 0.61 for deliberate practice and musical achievement.
limits: Competing readings of the same practice-skill correlation. Not independent confirmation.
agent_relevance: Time on task alone does not explain skill. Do not assume more passes or more compute alone yields expert quality.

source: Campitelli et al. (2015) editorial: transfer and general-cognition strand
finding: Reports that teaching experience is a very poor predictor of teacher effectiveness, that perceptual expertise with cars interferes with face processing, and that dance and climbing expertise are domain-bound. Chess education effects on academics are discussed through Bart (2014) and Gobet and Campitelli (2006).
numbers: No pooled numbers in the editorial; see later lines for the meta-analyses.
limits: Editorial only; the transfer claims are tested in the meta-analyses below.
agent_relevance: Warning for the agent: gains in one domain should not be expected to carry to others without shared structure.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017) Does far transfer exist? Negative evidence from chess, music and working memory training
finding: Two meta-analyses show chess players are about half an SD better on cognitive ability than non-players, and skill correlates with fluid intelligence, speed, working memory and knowledge. Three experimental meta-analyses of training in children find small overall effects that vanish with active controls.
numbers: Overall g: chess 0.34 [0.24,0.44]; music 0.16 [0.09,0.22]; WM training 0.12 [0.06,0.18]. Music: 0.25 (k=64) passive controls vs 0.03 [-0.07,0.12] (k=54) active controls. WM training: 0.18 (k=34) passive vs 0.05 [-0.05,0.15] (k=40) active. Chess: only one active-control study, effect 0.10. Near transfer of WM training to other memory tasks: 0.44 to 0.46 SD.
quote: The size of the effects was inversely related to the quality of the experimental design.
limits: Children and young adolescents only. Chess has too few active-control studies to be decisive. The authors are advocates of the common-elements view.
agent_relevance: The experts-are-smarter correlation does not mean practice builds general ability. Treat any claimed general boost from a skill as suspect unless tested against an active control.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017): theoretical frame (common elements, chunking, template theory)
finding: Thorndike and Woodworth's common-elements theory predicts near transfer often and far transfer rarely. Chunking and template theory say expert skill rests on tens of thousands of domain-specific chunks, hence little transfer. The authors say the meta-analyses support these theories and not the plasticity-based far-transfer hypothesis.
numbers: Action-video-game experiment cited: four games, improvements limited to the ability each game targeted.
limits: Argument from the authors; the neural-plasticity side is not tested here.
agent_relevance: The theory says what transfers: shared elements. A scaffold's transferable parts must be shared mechanics (check, compare, revise), not domain knowledge.

source: Sala & Gobet (2020) Cognitive and academic benefits of music training with children: a multilevel meta-analysis
finding: Updated music-training meta-analysis with Bayesian tests. The overall effect is near null once design quality is controlled. Small effects appear only without random allocation and with non-active controls.
numbers: N = 6,984, k = 254 effect sizes, m = 54 studies. Overall RVE g = 0.184 (SE 0.041); non-active controls 0.228; active controls 0.056 (SE 0.058; BF about 1.2). Sensitivity run: active -0.021 (SE 0.032, tau2 = 0); non-random 0.246 vs random 0.064 (SE 0.065).
limits: Children only. Earlier meta-analyses (Cooper: g = 0.28, 21 studies; Gordon: d = 0.20, 12 studies) were more positive.
agent_relevance: A second, larger test of the 2017 pattern: the better the control, the smaller the effect. In our own tests, compare against an active control (a different but plausible prompt), not just a bare baseline.

source: Sala & Gobet and colleagues (2023) Cognitive training: a field in search of a phenomenon (second-order meta-analysis)
finding: Second-order meta-analysis over 14 first-order meta-analyses finds near transfer is real but far transfer is null once placebo and publication bias are handled. Variance between training types is sampling error.
numbers: 332 samples, 1,555 effect sizes, 21,968 participants. Uncorrected far transfer: grand mean g = 0.12 (first-order range 0.04 to 0.19), true between-meta tau2 = 0. Corrected, active controls only: grand mean g = 0.00 (range -0.03 to 0.02). Examples: WM adults k=27 g=0.00; action video games k=34 g=-0.01; music children k=17 g=-0.02; chess children k=3 g=0.01.
quote: The overall effect of far transfer is null, and there is little to no true variability between the types of cognitive training.
limits: Written against Green et al. 2019 (48 researchers); the opposing camp disputes the artifact explanation. Chess has just 3 active-control samples.
agent_relevance: Strongest single statement of narrow transfer. Also warns that significant wins in a few runs are expected by chance even when the true effect is zero. Before adopting any scaffold operator, check that variance across items is not just sampling noise. About 5 percent of runs will look significant by chance.

source: Melby-Lervag, Redick & Hulme (2016) Working memory training does not improve performance on measures of intelligence or other measures of far transfer
finding: Meta-analysis of WM training with control groups. Immediate gains on trained and similar working-memory measures but no reliable far-transfer gains against treated controls. Publication-bias analysis found no evidential value with treated controls.
numbers: 87 publications, 145 experimental comparisons. Outcomes: nonverbal ability, verbal ability, word decoding, reading comprehension, arithmetic.
limits: Abstract only was read (Europe PMC record); full-text fetch failed.
agent_relevance: Mediation finding: bigger WM gains did not predict bigger far gains, so even real improvement in a component need not lift downstream skill.

source: Simons et al. (2016) Do brain-training programs work?
finding: Review of every study cited by brain-training companies. Training improves the trained tasks and sometimes closely similar tasks, but evidence for broad transfer to everyday cognition is weak, and many studies fell short of best-practice standards.
numbers: Context: 2014 consensus letter of 70+ scientists against brain games vs a counter-letter of 133 scientists.
limits: Abstract only was read.
agent_relevance: Frames the two camps and the best-practice list (active control, preregistered outcomes, expectation checks). Use the same list for agent evaluations: matched control prompt, blind scoring, preregistered metrics.

source: Boot, Blakely & Simons (2011) Do action video games improve perception and cognition?
finding: Lists methodological flaws that undermine the video-games-transfer-broadly claim: overt recruiting of gamers (demand characteristics), cross-sectional design (self-selection), no test of expectation differences, and active controls assumed to have equal placebo effects.
numbers: Only 2 published expert-novice gaming studies used covert recruiting (Donohue; Clark); both found a gamer advantage. Boot et al. 2008: 12 cognitive measures, little or no gamer advantage and no training benefit (Tetris and no-game controls). No published gaming study avoided all flaws.
quote: no published gaming study has successfully avoided them all.
limits: Perspective piece; no new data. Later meta-analyses give numbers.
agent_relevance: The control and expectation critique applies to prompt-scaffold comparisons where an expert-flavoured prompt may raise effort by suggestion.

source: Bediou et al. (2018) Meta-analysis of action video game impact on perceptual, attentional and cognitive skills
finding: Pro-transfer meta-analysis of studies from 2000 to 2015. Cross-sectional gamers beat non-gamers; intervention studies show a smaller effect, strongest for top-down attention and spatial cognition.
numbers: Cross-sectional g = 0.55. Intervention g = 0.34. Published effects estimated to be 30 percent larger than the full literature (publication bias). Authors ask for studies with more than 30 hours of training.
limits: Abstract only. Intervention controls were other commercial games. Contested by Sala et al.
agent_relevance: The best case for far transfer. Even here the effect shrinks from correlational to causal and again for bias. Use as the optimistic bound.

source: Sala, Tatlidil & Gobet (2018) Video game training does not enhance cognitive ability: a comprehensive meta-analytic investigation
finding: Three random-effects meta-analyses: game skill vs cognitive ability, players vs non-players, and training effects. All overall effects small or null; no evidence for a causal effect of gaming on general cognition.
numbers: k = 310 (skill-ability correlation), k = 315 (players vs non-players), k = 359 (training studies).
limits: Abstract only. Conflicts with Bediou et al. on the same literature, mainly through inclusion rules and control-group handling.
agent_relevance: Two meta-analyses of one literature disagree; the difference is how the control arm is defined. Fix the control rule in advance in our own tests.

source: van Ravenzwaaij et al. (2014) Action video games do not improve the speed of information processing in simple perceptual tasks (failed replication)
finding: Two training experiments tried to replicate Green, Pouget and Bavelier (2010), who used a diffusion model to claim faster information processing after action games. Action-game, cognitive-game and (Exp 2) no-game groups showed similar practice effects.
numbers: 5 supervised sessions per participant; Exp 2 added a no-game group. Sample sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only was read; first-author name given from memory, verify before citing.
agent_relevance: A failed replication of a famous perceptual-transfer claim. A reported improvement from a distinctive trainer may be a generic practice effect.

source: Gobet & Simon (1998) Expert chess memory: revisiting the chunking hypothesis
finding: A computerised replication of Chase and Simon (1973) with 26 players. The 2-second inter-piece interval still marks chunk boundaries, so chunks are real. Masters used far larger chunks than in 1973, which led to template theory.
numbers: N = 26: Masters n=5 (mean Elo 2453), Experts n=9 (2148), Class A n=12 (1869). Recall of game positions 92.0, 57.1, 32.2 percent; random positions 19.0, 13.8, 12.4 percent. Skill x position type F(2,23) = 34.17. Skill effect on random recall F(2,23) = 2.27, not significant. Largest chunk, Masters: 16.8 pieces in recall, 14 in copy; Chase and Simon's Master: 7. Random-position largest chunk about 4.6 (recall) and 6.3 (copy) for all skill levels.
limits: Small sample. Different apparatus from 1973 (screen not physical board). The random-position skill effect is small but found repeatedly in other studies.
agent_relevance: Expert advantage is huge when the stimulus is meaningful (about 3x pieces recalled) and small when scrambled (1.5x). This is the core evidence that expertise is domain-structured memory.

source: Gobet & Simon (1998): chunk count and the 50,000 estimate
finding: The 50,000-chunk figure is an extrapolation from the MAPP simulation (Simon and Gilmartin 1973; range 10,000 to 100,000). Holding argued 2,500 chunks might do if chunks coded relations, not locations. Mirror-image and translation tests degraded recall, which supports the larger number.
numbers: Chase and Simon 1973 first chunk replaced: Master 3.8 pieces, Class A 2.6, beginner 2.4; median largest Master chunk 5. In the new data the Master vs Class A difference in chunk number in recall is under one chunk.
limits: Chunk size, not chunk number, explains skill. Estimates are model-based, not measured directly.
agent_relevance: The chunk library is the part that cannot be transferred. The LLM analogue is pretraining coverage of a domain.

source: Gobet & Simon (1998): template theory and the CHREST lineage
finding: Template theory adds slots to frequently met chunks, so new information can be written into long-term memory in seconds. Slots hold piece locations and pointers to plans, moves and other templates. The same fast-write mechanism was proposed by Chase and Ericsson (1982) for digit-span experts.
numbers: Normal LTM learning rate quoted: 5 to 10 seconds per chunk; slot filling takes seconds.
limits: The computational form is the CHREST model; this paper reports the empirical test, not the full simulation.
agent_relevance: A formal model with testable predictions about what transfers: nothing without the same patterns. Slot filling resembles writing into a reusable template in context.

source: Holding & Reynolds (1982) via Gobet & Simon (1998): skill without memory for random positions
finding: Skill (1000 to 2200 Elo) did not correlate with recall of random positions shown briefly, yet skill did correlate with finding the best move in them. Gobet and Simon say pattern recognition applied recursively during look-ahead explains why a memory test alone can miss skill.
numbers: Elo range 1000 to 2200 in the original study.
limits: Secondhand through Gobet and Simon's review; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Skill shows in search quality even when recall of random input is flat. Measure the agent by what it does on domain problems, not by recall.

source: Sheridan & Reingold (2014) Expert vs novice differences in the detection of relevant information during a chess game: evidence from eye movements
finding: Experts fixate relevant board regions earlier than novices. The advantage shows in the first dwell and the first five fixations, not in total time, so it is fast detection, not more looking.
numbers: 41 players (df = 39); experts n = 17 (df = 16). Best move chosen on 93 percent of trials (SE 2) for experts vs 52 percent (SE 5) for novices, t(39) = 7.12. Move quality 9.5 vs 6.9 out of 10. Reaction time 28.9 s vs 41.9 s, p = 0.084. Expert RT correlated with Elo, r = -0.617. First-dwell fixations on relevant vs irrelevant regions: experts 2.19 vs 1.39, novices 2.05 vs 1.98. First-dwell interaction F(1,39) = 4.38; five-fixation 3-way interaction F(4,36) = 2.74. EyeLink 1000 at 1000 Hz; eight problems per player.
limits: Only correct trials analysed, so accuracy is matched. Total-time relevancy effects appeared in both groups. Experts were only marginally faster.
agent_relevance: Direct eye-tracking evidence that expert pattern memory steers attention within the first second or two. The agent could rank premises or regions by relevance first and spend its budget there.

source: Sheridan & Reingold (2014): earlier eye-tracking findings summarised in the introduction
finding: Charness et al. found experts (mean Elo 2238) put more fixations on best-move pieces than intermediates (Elo 1786) within the first five fixations. Reingold and Charness showed experts finish a perceptual-encoding phase (short fixations) and then switch to longer problem-solving fixations; intermediates stay in short fixations for 10 s.
numbers: Radiologists detect abnormalities in X-rays shown for 200 ms (Kundel and Nodine). Experts also show a larger visual span and parallel processing of chess configurations (Reingold et al.).
limits: Secondhand through the introduction; the original papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: The two-phase pattern (fast encode, then deliberate search) is a ready model for a staged agent loop.

source: Huan et al. (2025) Does math reasoning improve general LLM capabilities? Understanding transferability of LLM reasoning
finding: More than 20 open-weight reasoning models were audited on math, other reasoning and non-reasoning tasks. Most that succeed in math fail to transfer. In a controlled Qwen3-14B study, RL on math-only data transfers broadly while SFT on distilled math traces often loses general ability.
numbers: Qwen3-14B non-reasoning average: 45.7 base, 29.0 SFT no-think (transferability index -104.1), 53.2 RL. IFEval 69.2 base vs 41.4 SFT no-think vs 70.0 RL. Other-reasoning average 30.2 base vs 45.3 and 45.2 for SFT variants vs 60.0 RL.
quote: most models that succeed in math fail to transfer their gains to other domains.
limits: Table text was garbled by PDF extraction; sign of some index values should be checked against the figure. One model family in the controlled study.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of the narrow-transfer warning, with a twist: the training method, not the domain, decides whether skill transfers. Do not fine-tune on narrow traces expecting breadth.

source: Liu et al. (2026) SPIRAL: self-play on zero-sum games incentivizes reasoning
finding: Training LLMs by self-play on games (TicTacToe, Kuhn Poker, Simple Negotiation) improved reasoning benchmarks they never saw. This is the video-game-to-cognition transfer claim tested in models. Game training came close to maths RL on the same base model.
numbers: Qwen3-4B-Base average over 8 benchmarks: 34.0 base, 44.5 SPIRAL multi-game (+10.5), 46.0 RLVR on maths, 46.5 SPIRAL then RLVR. Qwen3-8B-Base 39.5 to 49.6 (+10.1). Octothinker-8B +8.0. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct +2.0. The paper reports SFT on 25,000 expert game trajectories at 38.4 average, below SPIRAL.
limits: Benchmarks are math and science QA, close in form to game reasoning. Gains may reflect RL eliciting latent base-model reasoning rather than game-specific skill. No active control with a non-game RL task was seen in the sections read.
agent_relevance: A striking contrast to human far-transfer nulls. A likely reason is that base models carry latent skill that any RL elicits, so the transfer is elicitation, not new structure. A scaffold can also elicit without training.

source: Xie et al. (2025) Play to generalize: learning to reason through game play (ViGaL)
finding: RL post-training of a 7B multimodal model on simple arcade games (Snake) improves maths (MathVista), multi-discipline (MMMU) and 3D spatial (VSI-Bench) benchmarks without worked solutions, and keeps general visual ability better than specialist models.
numbers: Abstract reports no numbers.
limits: Abstract page only; numbers not read.
agent_relevance: A second instance of game-to-reasoning transfer in models, with the same elicitation caveat as SPIRAL.

source: Aryabumi et al. (2024) To code, or not to code? Exploring impact of code in pre-training
finding: Including code in pretraining raises performance on non-code tasks: transfer in the other direction from the usual human null.
numbers: Models 470M to 2.8B parameters. Up to +8.2 percent relative in natural-language reasoning, +4.2 percent world knowledge, +6.6 percent generative win-rate, 12x code performance.
limits: Abstract page only. Relative gains; the ablation controls were not checked here. This is pretraining, not post-training.
agent_relevance: Transfer in LLMs follows shared structure in training data: code shares logic and format with reasoning text. This fits the common-elements account.

source: Betley et al. (2025) Emergent misalignment: narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs
finding: Finetuning models on insecure code, without telling the user, produced broad misaligned behaviour on unrelated prompts. When the user context was a security class, the effect did not occur. A backdoor trigger made the misalignment appear only with the trigger.
numbers: Strongest in GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct. Abstract gives no rates.
limits: Abstract page only. Behaviour was inconsistent: models were sometimes aligned.
agent_relevance: Counter-example to transfer being narrow: narrow training can spread widely when it changes the implied persona or intent. Role or style instructions in a scaffold may have wide side effects; test for them.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess
finding: A transformer of up to 270M parameters trained by supervised learning on Stockfish-annotated chess data plays at grandmaster level without explicit search. It predicts values for novel boards, but distilling Stockfish's search is not perfect.
numbers: ChessBench: 10 million games, 15 billion data points. Lichess blitz Elo 2895 against humans.
limits: Abstract page only. In-domain; says nothing about transfer to other domains.
agent_relevance: A machine analogue of chunk-based expertise: a very large domain-specific pattern store replaces search.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent world models and latent variable estimation in chess-playing language models
finding: A chess language model trained on next-character prediction builds an internal board representation found with linear probes and confirmed by interventions. It also encodes a latent skill level; adding a skill vector raised win rate by up to 2.6 times.
numbers: Up to 2.6x win rate with the skill vector.
limits: Abstract page only; probe accuracy not read.
agent_relevance: LLMs can represent player skill as a direction, which relates to prompting for expert behaviour. The effect shown is in-domain only.

source: Schut et al. (2023) Bridging the human-AI knowledge gap: concept discovery and transfer in AlphaZero
finding: Concepts extracted from AlphaZero were taught to four top grandmasters, who improved on concept prototype positions.
numbers: N = 4 grandmasters; no figures in the abstract.
limits: Abstract page only; tiny sample.
agent_relevance: Transfer of new chunks between experts works when concepts are shown through domain positions, not as general advice.
